newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Goodbye to national icons as EU banknotes unveiled.
newsitem.headline: Goodbye to national icons as EU banknotes unveiled.

text.p: Farewell the Eifel tower and James Joyce. Such symbols of national pride will be replaced by symbolic bridges and gateways on the euro bank note, the future single EU currency, which was unveiled in Dublin on Friday.

Undeterred by the date -- Friday the 13th is supposed to mean bad news in many EU states -- the winning design for the currency was made public while an EU summit a bus ride away was ironing out a pact supposed to defend the currency.
Alexandre Lamfalussy, head of the European Monetary Institute, forerunner of a future European Central Bank, told a news conference the choice of design was "clearly of major symblic significance."
The winning entry was designed by an Austrian Central Bank designer, Robert Kaliena, from 44 entries supposed to depict the "ages and styles of Europe" and modern abstract motifs.
It was selected amid great secrecy after a year-long competition contested by some 30 designer teams and Lamfalassy said the jury of 14 experts only told him the name of the winner two days ago.

The euro notes, in five, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200 and 500 euro denominations, range from grey to purple, differ slightly in size to help the partially sighted and blind, and feature no known landmark or personality.

Gone are national symbols such as the Atomium, a Brussels landmark which featured on the Belgian franc. Gone too are any human, historical figures such as the Irish writer James Joyce on the Irish punt currency -- or any people at all.

"We could not take monuments which depicted one country," Lamfalussy told the news conference. Instead, the notes feature a variety of imaginary bridges, windows and gateways and the EU's 12-star flag.

They are supposed to represent Europe's cultural history through its artistic ages - classical, romanesque, gothic, renaissance, baroque, rococo and the ages of iron and glass architecture and 20th century building styles.

"The design has been selected because it blends the historical development of the technical, artistic and communication fields in Europe in one harmonious composition and epitomises the dawn of a new common Europe with its common cultural heritage, and the vision of a common future in the next century, indeed, the new millennium" the EMI said.

The notes are supposed to replace the 12.5 billion bank notes in circulation among the bloc's 15 member states at present although exactly how many countries will be eligible to join the scheme has yet to be decided.

They were made public as the EU summit agreed after marathon talks on penalties against member states which stray from the strict borrowing limits enforced to turn the euro into a currency as solid as the German mark or swiss franc.
It is still not clear how many states will qualify or even want to qualify for monetary union.

Britain, Europe's perennial bad boy, says it will wait and see whether it joins. One fifth of the reverse side of the new notes has been left blank in case EU leaders decide they want to put national figures, such as the British Queen, on their notes.

Lamfalussy said the design was not 100 percent perfect and was going back to the designer's drawing board to fix some geographical blunders, such as the ommission on the map of Europe of countries like Cyprus and Turkey, which want to join the EU eventually.
"Part of his (the designer's) brief will be to ensure that the geograpjy is right. We have a number of problems, a few islands have disappeard. But we will take care of this," he said.
